content: Drooling, also known as ptyalism, sialorrhea, hypersalivation, or salivary hypersecretion, refers to the unintentional flow of saliva outside the mouth. This condition can arise due to neurological disorders or anatomical abnormalities of the oral cavity. It may result from excessive saliva production, weakened oral musculature that fails to retain saliva within the mouth, or difficulties in swallowing. Saliva is produced by the salivary glands, which are stimulated by excitatory signals from the salivary nuclei in the brainstem. These signals are triggered by taste and visual stimuli received from the tongue and other parts of the oral cavity. The salivary glands are categorized into major and minor glands. The major salivary glands include the parotid, submandibular, and sublingual glands, which are located at the base of the mouth, in front of the teeth, and in the cheeks. There are six major salivary glands in total, responsible for the majority of saliva secretion. Drooling is a common phenomenon in infants, often associated with teething, and typically resolves by 15 to 36 months of age as the child develops salivary continence. However, drooling in infants and young children can be exacerbated by upper respiratory infections and nasal allergies. Persistent sialorrhea beyond the age of four is considered pathological and may be due to hypersalivation, neurological disorders such as cerebral palsy, Parkinson’s disease, or amyotrophic lateral sclerosis, or as a side effect of certain medications. In children, cerebral palsy is the most common cause of sialorrhea, while in adults, Parkinson’s disease is the leading cause. Other contributing factors include dental malocclusion, postural issues, and an inability to recognize salivary spills. Drooling accompanied by fever or difficulty swallowing may indicate serious conditions such as retropharyngeal abscess, peritonsillar abscess, tonsillitis, mononucleosis, or strep throat. Sudden onset of drooling can also signal poisoning, particularly from pesticides, or reactions to snake or insect venom. Additionally, it may occur as a side effect of oral numbing agents or medications. Neurological problems and excessive intake of capsaicin, such as from high-Scoville-unit chili peppers, can also lead to drooling. Seasonal allergies caused by pollen, trees, grass, mold, and weeds may increase saliva production and contribute to drooling. Ptyalism can also occur during pregnancy, particularly in women with hyperemesis gravidarum, a condition characterized by severe nausea and vomiting. In such cases, excessive saliva production is a natural response to vomiting, but many women report difficulty swallowing the saliva, which exacerbates their symptoms. The complications of drooling are both physical and psychosocial. Physical issues include maceration and infection of the skin around the mouth, halitosis, dehydration, speech abnormalities, feeding difficulties, and an increased risk of aspiration of saliva, food, or fluids into the lungs, especially in individuals with impaired gag or cough reflexes. Psychosocially, drooling can lead to isolation, educational challenges, increased dependency, reduced self-esteem, and difficulty socializing, all of which significantly impact the quality of life. The physiology of saliva production involves the major salivary glands: the parotid, submandibular, and sublingual glands, with the parotid glands being the largest. Saliva aids in food lubrication and digestion, provides immunity, and maintains homeostasis in the body. Salivary secretion is primarily controlled by the parasympathetic nervous system, with minor contributions from the sympathetic nervous system. Parasympathetic fibers originating from the pons and medulla synapse in the otic and submandibular ganglia, regulating the functions of the parotid and submandibular/sublingual glands, respectively. Sympathetic signals assist in the contraction of muscle fibers surrounding the ducts of these glands, facilitating saliva flow. Approximately 1.5 liters of saliva are produced daily, with 90% of this output coming from the major salivary glands. In the basal state, 70% of saliva is produced by the submandibular and sublingual glands. Salivary secretion increases fivefold upon stimulation, with chewing being a significant stimulus. Salivary glands produce two types of saliva: thin, watery serous saliva (mainly from the parotid glands) and thick, viscous saliva (predominantly from the sublingual and submandibular glands). Excessive production of either type can cause problems, with watery saliva spilling from the mouth and viscous saliva being harder to clear, potentially causing choking and panic. The causes of drooling are diverse and include conditions such as retropharyngeal abscess, peritonsillar abscess, tonsillitis, mononucleosis, strep throat, Parkinson’s disease, epiglottitis, enlarged adenoids, poorly fitting dentures, Bell’s palsy, and cerebral palsy. Other causes include poisoning (e.g., pesticides), neurological disorders, infections, allergies, and anatomical abnormalities. Management of sialorrhea requires a multidisciplinary approach involving primary healthcare providers, speech therapists, occupational therapists, dentists, orthodontists, neurologists, and otolaryngologists. Treatment options range from conservative measures, such as observation, postural modifications, and biofeedback, to more aggressive interventions like medications, radiation, or surgical therapy. Anticholinergic medications, such as glycopyrrolate or scopolamine, effectively reduce drooling but may have side effects. Botulinum toxin type A injections into the parotid and submandibular glands are another safe and effective method, though the effects are temporary and require repeat injections. Surgical interventions, such as salivary gland excision, duct ligation, or rerouting, are the most effective and permanent treatment options, significantly improving patients’ quality of life. Home care for drooling due to teething includes maintaining good oral hygiene and using teething aids like frozen bagels, though care must be taken to avoid choking. Drooling is also common in children with neurological disorders or undiagnosed developmental delays. The underlying reasons for excessive drooling often include a lack of awareness of saliva buildup in the mouth, infrequent swallowing, and inefficient swallowing. Treatment focuses on increasing awareness of oral functions, improving swallowing frequency, and enhancing swallowing skills. Sialorrhea, characterized by drooling in the resting state, often results from open-mouth posture due to central nervous system depressants or side-sleeping. In this state, saliva may not accumulate at the back of the throat to trigger the normal swallow reflex, allowing drooling to occur. A comprehensive treatment plan for sialorrhea involves addressing reversible causes, behavior modification, medical treatment, and surgical procedures. Atropine sulfate tablets may be prescribed to reduce salivation, often in conjunction with behavior modification strategies. Surgical procedures are generally considered after evaluating non-invasive treatment options.
